s: Which one of the following institutions was established on a World Bank initiative and later became a universal bank?
o: Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India
x: ICICI was established in 1955 on a World Bank initiative and subsequently became a universal bank.

s: After LIC took majority control in 2019, as which type of bank was IDBI Bank reclassified?
x: Following LIC's majority acquisition in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a private sector bank.

s: Which of the following institutions was set up mainly to finance MSMEs?
x: SIDBI focuses on MSME finance. IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank finances export-import activity and ICICI gave private-sector industrial credit.

s: Which of the following institution–year of establishment pairs is correctly matched?
x: IDBI was set up in 1964. IFCI dates from 1948, ICICI from 1955 and SIDBI from 1990.

s: Why are development financial institutions (DFIs) important in the financial system?
o: They fill the long-term finance gap that banks cannot adequately meet because of asset-liability mismatch.
They provide only short-term working capital to retail borrowers.
They replace all NBFCs in providing microfinance.
x: DFIs fill the long-term finance gap because banks face an asset-liability mismatch in supplying long-term finance.

s: Which sector does NaBFID, India's newest development finance institution set up in 2021, finance?
x: NaBFID (2021) is the infrastructure DFI; SIDBI serves MSMEs, NHB housing and EXIM Bank trade.

s: When was SIDBI established?
x: SIDBI was set up on 2 April 1990; NABARD dates from 12 July 1982, NHB from 9 July 1988 and IFCI from 1 July 1948.

s: The National Housing Bank was set up in 1988 under the NHB Act of which year?
x: The NHB Act was passed in 1987 and the NHB was set up on 9 July 1988.

s: In which year were both IDBI and UTI established?
x: 1964 saw both IDBI and UTI set up; ICICI came in 1955 and LIC in 1956.

s: In which year was the Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), the first development finance institution, set up?
x: IFCI was set up on 1 July 1948 by a special Act; it was India's first DFI and its setting up began the era of development financing.

s: In which year was the Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank) set up?
x: EXIM Bank was set up in January 1982 to finance exports and imports; it is headquartered in Mumbai.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. IFCI, ICICI and IDBI all provided medium and long-term industrial finance.
2. IFCI was set up in 1964 under the RBI.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: IFCI, ICICI and IDBI all gave medium and long-term industrial finance. IFCI was set up in 1948; it was IDBI that was set up in 1964 under the RBI.

s: Which institution provides development and refinance support for loans to micro units?
x: MUDRA Bank gives development and refinance support for loans to micro units; NHB is for housing, EXIM for trade and NaBFID for infrastructure.

s: The National Housing Bank was set up on the advice of a high-level group headed by whom?
x: NHB (1988) was set up on the advice of the high-level group headed by C. Rangarajan; NABARD came from the Sivaraman Committee.

s: With what capital was NaBFID set up under the NaBFID Act, 2021?
x: NaBFID was set up with a capital of ₹20,000 crore, plus a grant of ₹5,000 crore.

s: IDBI was set up in 1964 under the RBI. In which year was it made autonomous?
x: IDBI began in July 1964 under the RBI and became autonomous in 1976.

s: What combined stake in IDBI Bank are the Government and LIC selling to a private buyer?
x: The Government and LIC are together selling a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank.

s: SIDBI began as a subsidiary of which institution?
x: SIDBI (1990) began as a subsidiary of IDBI.

s: Where is the headquarters of the Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank)?
x: EXIM Bank, set up in 1982 for export-import finance, has its head office in Mumbai.

s: Which was the second all-India term-lending institution to be set up in India?
x: IFCI (1948) was the first all-India term-lending institution and ICICI (1955) the second.

s:
Consider the following statements about NBFC-MFIs under the RBI microfinance framework (March 2022):
1. At least 75% of their assets must be in microfinance loans.
2. Microfinance loans must be backed by collateral.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is true: NBFC-MFIs must hold at least 75% of assets in microfinance loans. Statement 2 is false: microfinance loans are collateral-free.

s: Under the RBI microfinance framework (March 2022), up to what annual household income does a loan count as a microfinance loan?
x: A microfinance loan is a collateral-free loan to a household with annual income up to ₹3 lakh, repayment capped at 50% of income.

s: Under the RBI microfinance framework (March 2022), a household's loan repayments may not exceed what share of its income?
x: Microfinance repayments are capped at 50% of household income.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis of 2010:
1. The MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh expanded rapidly after the crisis.
2. It involved multiple lending and over-indebtedness.
3. Coercive recovery practices and borrower suicides marked it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh collapsed rather than expanding.

s: With whom did the Andhra Pradesh MFI Ordinance, 2010 require microfinance institutions to register?
x: The 2010 Ordinance required MFIs to register with district authorities; it also restricted doorstep recovery and capped interest.

s: After which event did the RBI set up the Malegam Committee?
o: formation of the first RRB in 1975
launch of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1992
x: The RBI constituted the Malegam Committee in 2010–11 after the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the Malegam Committee is correctly matched?
o: Lenders per borrower – no more than two MFIs
Lending proposed – unlimited lending by MFIs
x: The RBI's Malegam Committee proposed limiting lending to no more than two MFIs per borrower and a separate NBFC-MFI category; it did not back unlimited lending.

s: In March 2025, which lenders held the largest share of the microfinance loan portfolio?
x: In March 2025, NBFC-MFIs accounted for the largest share at 39%, followed by banks at 32%, SFBs at 16% and other NBFCs at 12%.

s: In which year was the Microfinance Industry Network (MFIN), the association of NBFC-MFIs, set up?
x: MFIN was set up in 2009; the RBI recognised it as a self-regulatory organisation in 2014.

s: Which two bodies did the RBI recognise as self-regulatory organisations for microfinance in 2014?
x: MFIN (the NBFC-MFI association, 2009) and Sa-Dhan were recognised as SROs in 2014.

s: About what share of microfinance borrowers in India are women?
x: About 95% of microfinance borrowers are women and 80% are rural.

s: In September 2018, the default of which entity set off a liquidity crisis in India?
o: National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development
x: Defaults by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited (IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.

s: In which year was the Unit Trust of India (UTI) established?
x: UTI was set up in 1964. LIC dates to 1956, GIC to 1972 and CRISIL to 1987.

s: In which year was the General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC) incorporated?
x: GIC was incorporated on 22 November 1972 under the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972; LIC dates from 1956.

s: Which of the following credit-rating agency–year pairs is correctly matched?
x: CRISIL was set up in 1987, ICRA in 1991 and CARE in 1993.

s: With which agency was ICRA, set up in 1991, a joint venture?
x: ICRA was set up in 1991 as a joint venture with Moody's.

s: In which year was the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) set up?
x: LIC was set up in 1956, before UTI (1964) and GIC (1972).

s: In which year was the credit-rating agency CARE set up?
x: CARE was set up in 1993; CRISIL came in 1987 and ICRA in 1991.

s: In which year did the Central Government take over the National Housing Bank, which was wholly owned by the RBI until then?
x: NHB was set up in 1988 and stayed wholly RBI-owned until the Central Government took over its ownership in 2019.

s: Which one of the following regulator–entity pairs is correctly matched?
x: Chit fund companies are regulated by the State Government. Merchant bankers are regulated by SEBI, insurance companies by IRDAI and NBFCs by RBI.

s: In which year was the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) Act enacted?
x: The IFSCA Act dates to 2019. The PFRDA Act is of 2013, the IRDA Act of 1999, and SEBI became statutory in 1992.

s: The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) began functioning in April 2020 as the regulator of which of the following?
o: all insurance companies and pension funds
International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City
x: IFSCA is the unified regulator for International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City, and began functioning in April 2020.

s: Under the Finance Act, 2019, to which body was the regulation of housing finance companies transferred from NHB?
o: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
x: The Finance Act, 2019 moved HFC regulation to the RBI; NHB retained supervision and refinance functions.

s: In which year was the PFRDA Act, which gives statutory backing to the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, enacted?
x: PFRDA regulates pensions and NPS under the PFRDA Act, 2013; 1999 is the IRDA Act and 2019 the IFSCA Act.

s: Who regulates merchant bankers in India?
x: SEBI regulates securities markets, FPIs, merchant bankers, venture capital and stock brokers.

s: In which year was the IRDA Act, under which the insurance regulator IRDAI works, enacted?
x: IRDAI regulates insurance companies under the IRDA Act, 1999.

s: When did the RBI grant a Certificate of Registration to the RMBS Development Company Limited (RDCL)?
x: RDCL received its RBI Certificate of Registration in January 2025; NHB contributed equity and it aims to develop the residential mortgage-backed securities market.

s: Which body launched RESIDEX, India's first official housing price index?
x: The NHB launched RESIDEX in July 2007.

s: After the IL&FS defaults, through whose order did the Government supersede the company's board?
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
x: Following the IL&FS defaults, the Government superseded its board through an NCLT order.

s: Which was the first financial services company to be resolved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC)?
x: DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC; Piramal acquired it in 2021.

s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
x: DHFL was acquired by Piramal in 2021, not 2019. The other pairs correctly associate IFCI, NaBFID and IL&FS with their stated milestones.

s: In which year did Piramal acquire DHFL under the IBC resolution?
x: DHFL, the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, was acquired by Piramal in 2021, not 2019.

s: In which type of financial institution did the default of IL&FS in September 2018 take place?
x: IL&FS was an infrastructure NBFC; its defaults in September 2018 set off a liquidity crisis among NBFCs (shadow lenders).

s: Under which section of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was DHFL, the first financial services company resolved under the IBC, taken up?
x: DHFL was resolved under Section 227 of the IBC, which covers financial service providers.

s: In which year was NABARD established?
x: NABARD was set up in 1982, on the Shivaraman Committee's advice. SIDBI followed in 1990.

s: The establishment of NABARD was based on the recommendations of which committee?
x: NABARD was established on the basis of the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations relating to CRAFICARD.

s: NABARD was set up on 12 July 1982 under an Act of which year?
x: NABARD was set up in 1982 under the NABARD Act, 1981.

s: Which body manages the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), funded by banks' priority-sector lending shortfalls?
x: NABARD manages RIDF, which is funded by banks' PSL shortfalls; it also refinances StCBs, RRBs and land development banks.

s:
Assertion (A): NABARD was established primarily for housing finance refinance.
Reason (R): NABARD took over the RBI's agricultural-credit functions and the refinance portfolio of ARDC.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: A is false: housing finance refinance is the purpose of NHB, not NABARD. R is true: NABARD took over the RBI's agricultural-credit functions and ARDC's refinance portfolio.

s: From which model is the group-lending idea of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme derived?
o: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh founded by Muhammad Yunus
x: The group-lending idea is associated with Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.

s: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by which law?
x: RRBs were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976. The BR Act 1949 is the general banking law, the NABARD Act 1981 created NABARD (which supervises RRBs), and the 1912 Act concerns cooperatives.

s: In which year did NABARD launch the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, called the world's largest microfinance movement, as a pilot?
x: NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme as a pilot in 1992. 1982 is NABARD's own establishment, 2006 is the JLG scheme, and 2010 is the AP microfinance crisis.

s: How many Regional Rural Banks are there in India now?
x: After amalgamations there are now 28 RRBs, governed by the RRB Act, 1976 and supervised by NABARD.

s:
Consider the following statements about NABARD's Joint Liability Group (JLG) scheme:
1. It mainly serves large landowning farmers.
2. It was launched in 2006.
3. A JLG usually has 4-10 members who give a mutual guarantee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: JLGs are mainly for tenant farmers and oral lessees.

s: Through which banks is the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme implemented?
o: Commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks
x: Commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks implement the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme launched by NABARD.

s: With which of the following is the Swabhimaan Scheme associated?
x: Swabhimaan was a scheme to take banking to rural areas.

s: Which of the following institutions performs a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies?
x: NHB plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.

s: For regulatory purposes, which of the following are classified by the Reserve Bank of India as refinance institutions?
x: RBI classifies NABARD, NHB and SIDBI as refinance institutions. EXIM Bank is classified as a term-lending institution.

s: To which class of institutions did LIC, UTI and GIC together belong?
x: LIC, UTI and GIC were the public-sector investment institutions.

s: Which of the following institutions are regulated and supervised by the Reserve Bank of India as All-India Financial Institutions?
o: IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, IIBI and LIC
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
NABARD, LIC, GIC, UTI and SIDCs
NHB, SIDBI, IFCI, TFCI and SFCs
x: The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.

s: Which of the following institutions was set up with the help of the Reserve Bank of India?
x: The RBI helped set up IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB; SEBI is not among them.

s: How many All-India Financial Institutions are regulated and supervised by the RBI?
x: The five RBI-regulated AIFIs are EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.

s: Which institution was added to the RBI-regulated AIFIs in 2022?
x: NaBFID joined EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB and SIDBI as an RBI-regulated AIFI in 2022.

s: Among the RBI-regulated AIFIs, how is EXIM Bank classed?
x: EXIM Bank is a term-lending institution; NABARD, NHB and SIDBI are the refinance institutions.

s: Which of the following was NOT set up with the help of the Reserve Bank of India?
x: IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, EXIM Bank and NEDB were set up with RBI help; SEBI was not.

s: Which institution acts as the quasi-regulator of State Financial Corporations?
x: SIDBI acts as quasi-regulator of State Financial Corporations, NABARD of RRBs and cooperatives, and NHB of HFCs.

s: Urban Cooperative Banks traditionally operated under which form of dual control?
o: State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and RBI
x: UCBs traditionally faced dual control by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and the RBI.

s: Which institution was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks?
x: NUCFDC was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks.

s: In the cooperative credit structure, which body provides short-term credit at the village level?
o: Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Bank
x: Village-level short-term credit comes from PACS; DCCBs work at the district level, StCBs at the state level, and PCARDBs give long-term credit at the village level.

s: State Cooperative Banks and DCCBs are licensed by the RBI. By whom are they inspected?
o: The State Registrar of Cooperative Societies
x: StCBs and DCCBs are licensed by the RBI and inspected by NABARD, while PACS fall under State Registrars.

s: After which event was the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 relating to UCBs enacted?
x: The amendment strengthening RBI supervision over UCBs followed the PMC Bank crisis.

s: What change in the licensing policy for Urban Cooperative Banks was indicated by the RBI?
o: Licensing restricted to multi-state cooperative banks only
Resumption of licensing on tap after a pause of more than two decades
Licensing transferred entirely to State Registrars
Permanent prohibition on new UCB licences
x: The RBI indicated that it would resume licensing UCBs on tap after a pause of more than two decades.

s: In the rural cooperative structure, which body provides long-term credit at the village level?
x: Primary Cooperative ARDBs give long-term credit at the village level; PACS give short-term credit.

s: Under whose control do Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) come?
x: PACS are under State Registrars; StCBs and DCCBs are licensed by the RBI and inspected by NABARD.

s: What is the name of NABARD's shared-services entity for cooperatives that received RBI approval?
x: The RBI approved NABARD's Sahakar Sarathi shared-services entity; NUCFDC is the umbrella body for UCBs.

s: How many Urban Cooperative Banks were there in India in August 2026?
x: There were 1,457 UCBs as on 6 August 2026.

s: What is the main source of short-term funds for NBFCs?
x: Liquid debt mutual funds are the main short-term funders of NBFCs, which cannot take demand deposits or use the LAF.

s: In which of the following is Foreign Direct Investment prohibited in India?
x: FDI is prohibited in chit funds and Nidhi companies, which belong to the unorganised segment; insurance, banking and pensions allow FDI within limits.

s: Into which scheme was the NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 later merged?
x: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was merged into the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021.

s:
Consider the following statements about the principal business test for NBFCs:
1. Financial assets must exceed 50% of total assets.
2. Financial income must exceed 50% of gross income.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are true: an NBFC meets the 50-50 test when financial assets exceed 50% of total assets and financial income exceeds 50% of gross income.

s: What is the minimum net owned fund required for a housing finance company (HFC)?
x: HFCs need a minimum NOF of ₹20 crore, against ₹10 crore for NBFC-MFIs and NBFC-ICCs.

s: Under the Scale-Based Regulation framework, which is the correct order of the four NBFC layers from lower to higher regulatory intensity?
x: The four layers are Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and Top Layer, with regulation increasing across the framework.

s: When is the Top Layer under Scale-Based Regulation meant to be used?
o: there is a sharp rise in systemic risk
x: The Top Layer is kept empty in normal circumstances and is intended for a sharp rise in systemic risk.

s: Under Scale-Based Regulation, within how many years must an NBFC identified by the RBI for the Upper Layer get listed?
x: Upper Layer NBFCs are identified by the RBI, follow bank-like norms for at least five years and must list within three years.

s: Which one of the following companies was specifically included in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27?
x: Tata Sons was included among the 17 companies named in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27.

s: Which of the following pairs of entity and classification is INCORRECTLY matched?
x: CIC, IFC and HFC are listed NBFC categories; a Regional Rural Banking Company is not an NBFC category (RRBs come under the RRB Act, 1976).

s: To what amount is the minimum net owned fund for an NBFC-ICC being raised from ₹2 crore?
x: NBFC-ICCs move from ₹2 crore to ₹10 crore NOF on a glide path to March 2027; ₹20 crore is the HFC requirement.

s: Under which law are NBFCs in India registered?
x: NBFCs are companies registered under the Companies Act and regulated by the RBI.

s: For at least how many years must an NBFC placed in the Upper Layer follow bank-like norms?
x: An Upper Layer NBFC follows bank-like norms for at least 5 years and must list within 3 years.

s: Which category of NBFC, introduced by the RBI in 2017, runs online platforms for peer-to-peer lending?
x: NBFC-P2P (2017) are RBI-regulated online platforms where individuals lend directly to borrowers.

s: How many companies were placed in the RBI's NBFC Upper Layer list for 2026-27?
x: The NBFC-UL list for 2026-27 has 17 companies, including Tata Sons (up from 15 in April 2026).

s: Which one of the following is true of NBFCs in India?
o: They cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves
They have access to the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility
x: An NBFC cannot issue cheques drawn on itself. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, their deposits have no insurance cover, and they have no LAF access.

s: Which of the following about reserve requirements is NOT correct?
x: NBFCs do not maintain CRR; banks maintain CRR and SLR, while deposit-taking NBFCs maintain liquid assets instead.

s: Which of the following activities is NOT permitted to Payments Banks?
o: Accepting deposits within the permitted framework
x: Payments Banks cannot lend. Their role includes deposits and payment services, but not credit provision.

s: Unlike banks, NBFCs are NOT part of which of the following?
x: Banks are part of the payment and settlement system; NBFCs are not, though they are RBI-regulated companies.

s:
Consider the following statements about NBFCs in India:
1. They cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.
2. Their deposits are covered by DICGC deposit insurance.
3. They have no access to the RBI's LAF (repo) window.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: DICGC deposit insurance covers banks, not NBFCs.

s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of instruments or markets associated with the organised financial system?
o: Artisans, farmers, small traders and nidhis
Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit
Indigenous bankers, chit funds, nidhis and moneylenders
Unregulated loan companies, repo, nidhis and moneylenders
x: Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit are components of the organised financial system. The other sets include unorganised institutions or users.

s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of indigenous bankers?
o: Chit funds, loan companies, moneylenders and RRBs
x: Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.

s: Which laws govern professional and agricultural moneylenders in India?
o: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
x: Moneylenders fall under state money-lending laws; the Chit Funds Act, 1982 relates to chit funds.

s: Which of the following belongs to the unorganised money market?
o: Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper
x: Indigenous bankers and moneylenders form part of the unorganised money market. T-Bills, commercial bills, CDs, CPs and repos belong to the organised segment.

s: What does the term 'regulatory arbitrage' refer to in the context of shadow banking?
o: The transfer of cooperative banks to the stock market
The allocation of all public debt to development finance institutions
The compulsory conversion of every NBFC into a bank
Using differences in regulatory treatment to conduct financial activities outside the stricter banking framework
x: Regulatory arbitrage describes the use of differences in regulatory treatment to conduct activities through less strictly regulated financial entities, a criticism associated with shadow banking.

s: Which of the following lies outside India's organised money market?
o: Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI)
x: The 2017 key treated finance companies as outside the organised money market; commercial banks, DFHI and cooperative banks are RBI-regulated constituents of it.

s: Who regulates chit funds in India?
x: Chit funds are regulated by the State Government under the Chit Funds Act, 1982, not by the RBI.

s: Who coined the term 'shadow banking' in 2007?
x: US economist Paul McCulley coined 'shadow banking' in 2007 for bank-like credit intermediation outside full bank regulation.

s: In which instrument do indigenous bankers in India typically deal?
x: Indigenous bankers such as Shroffs and Chettiars combine banking with trade and deal in hundis; T-bills and CDs belong to the organised market.

s: Which of the following describes an indigenous banker?
o: Accepts deposits and lends, while also combining banking with trade or commission business
Provides only long-term loans to infrastructure companies
Operates exclusively under the supervision of the RBI
Only lends in kind and does not accept deposits
x: An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, while combining banking activities with trade or commission business. Shroffs and Mahajans are examples.

s: In which year was the Andhra Pradesh Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies (MACS) Act enacted?
x: The AP MACS Act dates from 1995; the AP Cooperative Societies Act dates from 1964.

s: Which statement correctly describes the jurisdiction of the AP Cooperative Tribunal?
o: It has only advisory jurisdiction under both Acts.
It has original jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and appellate jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It has appellate jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It exercises jurisdiction only over Urban Cooperative Banks.
x: Under Section 75 of the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964, the Tribunal is appellate under that Act and has original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.

s: Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank was formed through the merger of how many Regional Rural Banks?
x: It was formed by merging four RRBs: Andhra Pragathi, Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas, Chaitanya Godavari and Saptagiri Grameena Banks.

s: According to the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26, how many DCCBs operate in Andhra Pradesh?
x: AP has 13 DCCBs with 436 branches; APCOB has 18 branches.

s: Under which section of the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964 is the Cooperative Tribunal provided?
x: Section 75 of the 1964 Act provides an appellate Cooperative Tribunal; under the MACS Act 1995 the tribunal has original jurisdiction.

s: Which of the following was NOT among the RRBs merged into Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank?
x: AP Grameena Bank merged Andhra Pragathi, AP Grameena Vikas, Chaitanya Godavari and Saptagiri Grameena Banks.

s: According to the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26, how many PACS are there in Andhra Pradesh?
x: AP has APCOB, 13 DCCBs and 2,024 PACS.

s: Who signs the one-rupee note in India?
x: The one-rupee note carries the Finance Secretary's signature; all other RBI notes are signed by the RBI Governor.

s: Which currency function is performed by the Government of India and NOT by the RBI?
x: Coins are minted by the Government of India; the RBI issues banknotes (except the ₹1 note) and exchanges and destroys unfit notes.

s: Who issues coins in India?
x: The Government of India (Ministry of Finance) issues coins and the ₹1 note; the RBI issues all other notes.

s: Who issues the ₹1 note in India?
o: The Government of India (Ministry of Finance)
x: The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India through the Ministry of Finance, which also issues coins; the RBI issues the other notes.

s: Under the Minimum Reserve System, what minimum reserve must the RBI maintain?
x: Under the Minimum Reserve System, as amended in 1957, the RBI must keep at least ₹200 crore of gold and foreign exchange, of which ₹115 crore must be gold. The system itself replaced the Proportional Reserve System in 1956.

s: What is the highest denomination of currency note permitted under Section 24 of the Reserve Bank of India Act?
x: Section 24 of the RBI Act permits a highest denomination of ₹10,000.

s: Under which section of the Reserve Bank of India Act is the power to demonetise bank notes exercised?
x: Section 26(2) of the RBI Act provides the power relating to demonetisation of bank notes.

s: Which of the following correctly represents the denominations withdrawn from circulation during the 2016 demonetisation?
x: On 8 November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes were demonetised.

s: What is the legal status of the ₹2,000 note withdrawn from circulation in May 2023?
o: Ceased to be legal tender immediately
Is legal tender only for banks
x: The ₹2,000 note was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 but continues to have legal-tender status.

s: Indian currency notes carry how many languages in total?
x: Indian currency notes carry 17 languages in total: Hindi and English on the front and 15 scheduled languages in the language panel on the back.

s: What is the legal tender status of coins issued by the Government of India?
o: Legal tender only when specifically notified
x: Coins are limited legal tender, whereas every RBI note is unlimited legal tender.

s: The 1978 demonetisation withdrew notes of which denominations?
x: The 1978 HDBN Demonetisation Act withdrew ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes; 2016 withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000.

s: By what majority did the Supreme Court uphold the 2016 demonetisation in 2023?
x: The Supreme Court upheld the 8 November 2016 demonetisation by a 4:1 majority in 2023.

s: The assets that back the note issue of the RBI are specified in which section of the RBI Act?
x: Section 33 lists the assets backing notes, held in the Issue Department; Section 24 sets the highest denomination.

s: The RBI's MANI app, launched in 2020, helps:
o: Visually impaired persons identify currency notes
x: MANI (Mobile Aided Note Identifier) helps the visually impaired identify currency notes.

s: How many languages appear in the language panel at the back of Indian currency notes?
x: Notes carry 17 languages: Hindi and English in front and a language panel of 15 at the back.

s: Which of the following about Indian currency is NOT correct?
o: RBI notes are unlimited legal tender
The ₹1 note is signed by the Finance Secretary
Coins are issued by the Government of India
x: Coins are only limited legal tender; RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, and the ₹1 note is a Government issue signed by the Finance Secretary.

s: In which year did India move from the Proportional Reserve System to the Minimum Reserve System for note issue?
x: The Proportional Reserve System was replaced by the Minimum Reserve System in 1956; the minimum was revised to ₹200 crore in 1957.

s: In which year was the ₹10,000 note first printed in India?
x: The ₹10,000 note was first printed in 1938, demonetised in 1946, revived in 1954 and demonetised again in 1978.

s: Under the Proportional Reserve System followed till 1956, what share of the backing for note issue had to be in gold or sterling?
x: Under the Proportional Reserve System, 2/5 of the backing had to be gold or sterling, with gold of at least ₹40 crore.

s: When the Minimum Reserve System was introduced in 1956, what minimum reserve was fixed?
x: In 1956 the minimum reserve was ₹515 crore (₹400 crore foreign securities + ₹115 crore gold); it was cut to ₹200 crore in 1957.

s: After being demonetised in 1946, in which year was the ₹10,000 note brought back?
x: The ₹10,000 note, first printed in 1938, was demonetised in 1946, revived in 1954 and demonetised again in 1978.

s: Up to what denomination can coins be issued under the Coinage Act?
x: Coins are limited legal tender and can be issued up to ₹1,000 under the Coinage Act.

s: Under which provision of the Reserve Bank of India Act does the RBI have the sole right to issue banknotes, subject to the exception of the one-rupee note?
x: Section 22 of the RBI Act confers the sole right to issue banknotes on the RBI, except for the one-rupee note.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the RBI's role as banker, agent and adviser to governments?
o: Section 20 relates to the RBI's business with the Central Government
Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts are unrelated to this function
Sections 21 and 21A relate to State Governments
The RBI manages public debt through its Public Debt Office
x: Ways and Means Advances and overdrafts are part of the RBI's government-banking function, so that statement is false; the others are correct.

s: Under which Act does the RBI regulate payment systems in India?
x: Payment systems are regulated by the RBI under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

s:
Assertion (A): The RBI acts as the Lender of Last Resort for banks.
Reason (R): The RBI provides emergency liquidity to banks when required.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true: the RBI is the lender of last resort because it gives banks emergency liquidity when no one else will. R explains A.

s: Which of the following pairs of RBI function and role is correctly matched?
o: Payment systems – Management of foreign exchange reserves
Banker to Government – Oversight of payment systems
Controller of credit – Controls money and credit through monetary policy
x: As controller of credit the RBI runs monetary policy. As banker to Government it handles transactions and public debt; it also manages forex reserves and oversees payment systems.

s: Which of the following pairs of RBI role and its content is correctly matched?
o: Banker to banks – accepts deposits from the public
Banker to banks – mints coins for commercial banks
Banker to banks – holds commercial banks' deposits and reserves
Banker to banks – creates credit for the public
x: The RBI is the bankers' bank because commercial banks keep their deposits and reserves with it; it does not take public deposits, mint coins or create credit.

s: The RBI acts as banker to the Central Government under which section of the RBI Act?
x: Section 20 covers the Centre; Sections 21/21A cover States by agreement; Section 22 is note issue.

s: The RBI is banker to all State Governments except which one?
x: Sikkim has only a limited agreement with the RBI, for public debt; the RBI is banker to all other States.

s: Under which body does the Public Debt Office, which manages government borrowing, function?
x: The Public Debt Office functions under the RBI as banker to the Government.

s: What is the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks or rediscounts their bills called?
x: The Bank Rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to or rediscounts bills of commercial banks.

s: Under which Act does the RBI manage India's foreign exchange reserves?
x: As custodian of forex, the RBI manages India's foreign exchange reserves under FEMA, 1999.

s: Which development gave the Reserve Bank of India operational independence in determining policy rates while retaining the statutory monetary policy framework?
o: The 2016 Monetary Policy Committee and inflation-targeting law
The 2007 Payment and Settlement Systems Act
The 2019 transfer of ownership of NHB
x: The MPC framework and inflation-targeting law introduced in 2016 gave the RBI operational independence on policy rates.

s: What is the primary objective of the RBI's monetary policy?
x: The RBI's monetary policy gives primary importance to price stability, while keeping growth in consideration.

s: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of India have?
x: The MPC is a six-member statutory body under the RBI Act that sets the policy repo rate.

s: In India's monetary-policy framework, who sets the inflation target?
o: The Finance Ministry, in consultation with the RBI
x: The Finance Ministry sets the inflation target in consultation with the RBI; the RBI frames and implements monetary policy and the MPC fixes the repo rate.

s: On which date were interest rates on savings bank accounts in India deregulated?
x: Savings rates were deregulated on 25 October 2011; the RBI no longer fixes them or banks' PLR.

s:
Arrange in chronological order:
1. Nationalisation of the RBI
2. Appointment of the Hilton Young Commission
3. Passing of the RBI Act
4. RBI starts functioning
x: Hilton Young Commission (1926), RBI Act (1934), RBI begins operations (1935), nationalisation (1949).

s: In which year was the Central Office of the Reserve Bank of India shifted from Calcutta to Bombay?
x: The RBI’s Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in 1937.

s: Under which Act was the Reserve Bank of India nationalised?
x: The RBI was nationalised under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948, with effect from 1 January 1949.

s: When did the Reserve Bank of India begin functioning?
x: The RBI began work on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934; it was nationalised with effect from 1 January 1949.

s: What does the seal of the Reserve Bank of India depict?
o: an elephant and a banyan tree
a lion and a palm tree
a tiger and a palm tree
x: The RBI seal contains a tiger and a palm tree. The tiger replaced the lion in the East India Company double-mohur design.

s: In which year did B.R. Ambedkar give the evidence to the Hilton Young Commission that shaped the idea of the RBI?
x: Ambedkar's 1925 evidence to the Hilton Young Commission shaped the RBI; the Commission recommended a central bank in 1926.

s: On which date did the RBI mark its 90th year (RBI@90)?
x: RBI@90 fell on 1 April 2024, as the RBI began functioning on 1 April 1935; 1 April 2020 was the 85th Foundation Day.

s: Since 2020-21, what is the accounting year of the RBI?
x: The RBI moved from July–June to April–March from 2020-21, with a nine-month transition year (July 2020–March 2021).

s: The tiger on the RBI's seal replaced which animal of the East India Company double mohur?
x: The RBI seal shows a tiger and palm tree; the tiger replaced the lion of the East India Company double mohur.

s: In which year did the Hilton Young Commission recommend the setting up of a central bank for India?
x: The Hilton Young Commission recommended a central bank in 1926; the RBI Act followed in 1934 and the RBI began in 1935.

s: By what other name was the Hilton Young Commission known?
o: Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance
x: The Hilton Young Commission (1926) was the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, on whose advice the RBI was set up.

s: Which of the following about the Reserve Bank of India is NOT correct?
o: It was originally headquartered in Kolkata
It became fully government-owned after nationalisation
Its head office is now in Mumbai
x: The RBI was nationalised in 1949, not 1937; 1937 is when its head office moved from Kolkata to Mumbai.

s: For how many years do directors of the RBI's Central Board hold office?
x: The Central Board has 21 members and its directors hold office for 4 years; the Governor and Deputy Governors serve up to 5 years.

s: Who was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?
x: C. D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor of the RBI, serving from 1943 to 1949.

s: Who was the first Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?
x: Sir Osborne Smith was the first RBI Governor (1935-37); he signed no Indian note because King Edward VIII had abdicated.

s: Who has been the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India since December 2024?
x: Sanjay Malhotra has been RBI Governor since December 2024 and chairs the MPC and the Payments Regulatory Board; Shaktikanta Das was Governor 2018-2024.

s: Of the four Deputy Governors of the RBI, how many are usually drawn from within the RBI's own ranks?
x: The usual composition is two from within the RBI, one commercial banker and one economist who heads monetary policy.

s: Which one of the following is NOT an autonomous institute associated with the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research
Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology
x: NIBM, IGIDR and IDRBT are autonomous institutes. The Reserve Bank Staff College is a training college, not an autonomous institute in this classification.

s:
Consider the following statements about the governance of the RBI:
1. Its Central Board of Directors has 21 members.
2. Directors of the Central Board hold office for 5 years.
3. The Governor is appointed by the Government of India for up to 5 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: Board directors hold office for 4 years.

s: Among the four RBI Deputy Governors, which area does the economist usually head?
x: The four Deputy Governors are two from within the RBI, one commercial banker and one economist who heads monetary policy.

s: The RBI's Andhra Pradesh regional office began on 22 August 2022. To which city did it move in 2025?
x: The AP regional office first worked from Hyderabad and moved to Vijayawada in 2025; AP currency work stays with Hyderabad.

s: Who was Governor of the Reserve Bank of India from 1992 to 1997?
x: C. Rangarajan was Governor in 1992-97; Manmohan Singh served 1982-85 and Bimal Jalan 1997-2003.

s:
Arrange the following RBI Governors in chronological order:
1. Bimal Jalan
2. Manmohan Singh
3. C. Rangarajan
4. C. D. Deshmukh
x: C. D. Deshmukh (1943-49), Manmohan Singh (1982-85), C. Rangarajan (1992-97) and Bimal Jalan (1997-2003).

s: Where is the Reserve Bank Staff College, a training institution of the RBI, located?
x: The Reserve Bank Staff College is in Chennai; the College of Agricultural Banking is in Pune.

s: Who was appointed Deputy Governor of the RBI in May 2026 for three years, replacing T. Rabi Sankar?
x: Rohit Jain was appointed RBI Deputy Governor in May 2026 for three years in place of T. Rabi Sankar.

s: Where is the College of Agricultural Banking of the RBI located?
x: The RBI's College of Agricultural Banking is at Pune; the Reserve Bank Staff College is at Chennai.

s: How many Local Boards does the Reserve Bank of India have?
x: The RBI has four Local Boards (Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, New Delhi), each sending one director to the Central Board.

s: Which of the following cities is NOT the seat of a Local Board of the RBI?
x: The four Local Boards are at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and New Delhi; Hyderabad has none.

s: Who operates the Government of India's mints at Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata and Hyderabad?
x: SPMCIL operates the Government of India's four mints; they are not owned by the RBI.

s: Where is the Bank Note Press located?
x: The Bank Note Press is at Dewas; the Currency Note Press is at Nashik, and the RBI-owned BRBNMPL presses are at Mysuru and Salboni.

s: Where are the RBI-owned BRBNMPL note presses located?
x: BRBNMPL presses are at Mysuru (Karnataka) and Salboni (West Bengal); Nashik and Dewas are SPMCIL presses.

s: Where is the Currency Note Press of SPMCIL located?
x: The Currency Note Press is at Nashik; Dewas has the Bank Note Press.

s: Which of the following cities does NOT have a SPMCIL mint?
x: The four mints are at Mumbai, Noida, Kolkata and Hyderabad; Nashik has the Currency Note Press, not a mint.

s: Who chairs the Payments Regulatory Board (PRB)?
x: The PRB is chaired by the RBI Governor; it has six members, replaced the BPSS and draws its powers from the PSS Act, 2007.

s: Non-Banking Financial Companies are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India under which chapter of the RBI Act?
x: NBFCs are regulated under Chapter IIIB of the Reserve Bank of India Act.

s: Under Section 26A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, deposits unclaimed for how long are transferred to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund?
x: Deposits unclaimed for ten or more years go to the DEA Fund, but the depositor's right to claim survives.

s: Payments banks are licensed under which provision of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949?
x: Payments banks are licensed under Section 22(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

s: What share of new branches must be in unbanked rural areas for banks to open branches without prior RBI approval?
x: The general permission is subject to at least 25% of new branches being in unbanked rural areas; it also covers SFBs, payments banks, LABs and RRBs.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Approval of bank amalgamations — Reserve Bank of India
Winding up of every bank without legal process — Reserve Bank of India
Licensing of all insurance companies — Reserve Bank of India
Conduct of monetary policy by commercial banks — Reserve Bank of India
x: The RBI approves amalgamations of banks and can seek the winding up of a bank. The other functions are either overstated or belong to other institutions.

s: Which RBI committee deals specifically with cyber security?
x: The RBI's Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee deals with cyber security matters.

s: The Reserve Bank Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) 2026, effective from 1 July 2026, is based on which principle?
x: RB-IOS 2026 follows the principle of “One Nation, One Ombudsman” and covers banks, RRBs, UCBs, NBFCs and payment operators.

s: In which year was the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) set up under the RBI?
x: BFS was set up in 1994 for integrated supervision of banks, financial institutions and NBFCs.

s: Under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, who approves mergers of banks?
x: The BR Act gives the RBI power over licensing, branches and amalgamation; mergers are approved by the RBI.

s: Which body did the RBI's Payments Regulatory Board replace?
o: Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems
x: The six-member PRB, set up in October 2025, replaced the BPSS and draws its powers from the PSS Act, 2007.

s: With which subject did the Tarapore Committee (1997; 2006) of the RBI deal?
x: The Tarapore Committee dealt with capital account convertibility; cyber security is with the Inter-disciplinary Standing Committee.

s: How many members does the RBI's Payments Regulatory Board have?
x: The Payments Regulatory Board has six members, is chaired by the RBI Governor and has three Government nominees.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Reserve Bank Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS), 2026:
1. It came into force on 1 July 2026.
2. It puts no cap on the amount of a complaint.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: RB-IOS 2026 ('One Nation One Ombudsman') began on 1 July 2026 and has no cap on the amount.

s: The Reserve Bank of India recorded a surplus of approximately what amount for the financial year 2025–26?
x: The RBI recorded a surplus of ₹2.86 lakh crore for 2025–26, described as its highest-ever surplus.

s: Under Section 7 of the RBI Act, the Central Government may give directions to the RBI in the public interest after consulting whom?
x: Section 7 allows the Central Government to issue directions to the RBI in the public interest after consulting the RBI Governor.

s: Under which provision is the net profit of the Reserve Bank of India, after making provisions, transferred to the Central Government?
x: Section 47 of the RBI Act provides for transferring the net profit remaining after provisions to the Central Government.

s: Under which section of the RBI Act can the Central Government supersede the RBI's Central Board?
x: Section 30 lets the Government supersede the Central Board. Section 7 allows directions after consulting the Governor, Section 22 gives the sole right of note issue, and Section 47 covers transfer of surplus profit.

s: Under which Article does the President constitute the Finance Commission?
x: The Finance Commission is formed by the President under Article 280; it is not an RBI body.

s: Which of the following is NOT a source of income of the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Interest on domestic and foreign securities
Income tax collected from individual taxpayers
x: RBI income includes interest on securities and loans, foreign exchange gains and fees. Collection of income tax from individual taxpayers is not an RBI income source.

s: Under the revised Economic Capital Framework (2025), within what band is the RBI's Contingent Risk Buffer maintained?
x: The CRB band was revised in 2025 to 4.5%–7.5% of the balance sheet; the earlier band was 5.5%–6.5%.

s: The Bimal Jalan Committee's Economic Capital Framework primarily sought to distinguish between which of the following?
x: The framework distinguished realised equity from revaluation balances and provided for a Contingent Risk Buffer.

s: Before its 2025 revision, what was the RBI's Contingent Risk Buffer band under the Jalan framework?
x: The Bimal Jalan Committee set the CRB at 5.5–6.5%; the 2025 revision widened it to 4.5–7.5%.

s: Which of the following institutions was set up with the help of the RBI?
x: The RBI helped set up IDBI, NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB; SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA are separate regulators.

s:
Consider the following statements about the RBI's developmental role:
1. The RBI helped set up NABARD and EXIM Bank.
2. Ownership of the institutions it helped set up still rests with the RBI.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: ownership of IDBI, NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB later moved to the Government.

s: Which one of the following is classified as a contingent function of money?
x: The contingent functions include acting as a basis of credit, distribution of national income and giving liquidity.

s: Which one of the following is an example of near money?
o: Currency notes held by the public
x: Time deposits are highly liquid assets but cannot directly be used to pay for goods and services, making them near money. Other examples include Treasury bills, bills of exchange and savings certificates.

s: Which one of the following statements about legal tender is NOT correct?
o: Every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender.
RBI notes are unlimited legal tender anywhere in India.
A creditor is legally bound to accept legal tender in settlement of a claim.
x: Not every highly liquid financial asset is legal tender; near money such as time deposits and Treasury bills cannot directly settle ordinary payments. RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, while coins are limited legal tender.

s: Which one of the following is NOT legal tender in India?
o: Currency notes issued by the RBI
x: Plastic money (debit/credit cards) is not legal tender. RBI notes are unlimited legal tender, coins are limited legal tender, and the Digital Rupee is legal tender under the RBI Act as amended by the Finance Act 2022.

s: 'Store of value' is classified as which type of function of money?
x: Store of value is a secondary function; medium of exchange is primary and basis of credit is contingent.

s: By what is 'hard money' backed?
x: Hard money is backed by gold or credible assets; soft money is paper money backed by government bonds.

s: Which enactment amended the RBI Act to make the Digital Rupee legal tender?
x: The RBI Act was amended by the Finance Act 2022 to make the Digital Rupee legal tender.

s: Which of the following is NOT a contingent function of money?
x: Medium of exchange is a primary function; basis of credit, distribution of national income and giving liquidity are contingent functions.

s: Bank money, as distinct from cash, is also known as which type of money?
x: Bank money is secondary money, while cash is high-powered money; together currency and deposit money make up money supply.

s: By what is 'soft money' backed?
x: Soft money is paper money backed by government bonds; hard money is backed by gold or credible assets.

s: What does velocity of money refer to?
o: the average number of times a unit of currency changes hands during a period
the total quantity of currency printed by the central bank in a year
the percentage of bank deposits kept as reserves
the rate at which coins are minted by the government
x: Velocity is the average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a given period. A ₹10 note used twice generates ₹20 of transactions.

s: A ₹500 note costs about ₹4 to produce. What is the difference between its face value and production cost called?
x: Seigniorage is the difference between the face value of currency and its cost of production. It represents the issuer's profit and is a source of RBI surplus.

s: Why is a rupee coin called a token coin?
o: Its metal value is higher than its face value.
It can be used only for token payments.
Its face value is higher than the value of the metal contained in it.
It is not issued under government authority.
x: A rupee coin is a token coin because its face value exceeds the value of the metal contained in it.

s: What are notes and coins that have no intrinsic value and are money by government order called?
x: Fiat money has no intrinsic value; it is money because the government orders it.

s: What is the fixed percentage of deposits that every bank must keep as reserves called?
x: The Required Reserve Ratio is the fixed share of deposits every bank must keep as reserves.

s: What happens to the value of money when currency expands?
x: Currency expansion lowers the value of money, so prices rise.

s: If a ₹10 note changes hands twice in a period, what value of transactions does it support?
x: Velocity is the number of times money changes hands; ₹10 used twice supports ₹20 of transactions.

s: Which denominations were covered by the 1978 demonetisation?
x: The High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978, under Morarji Desai, withdrew the ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes to curb black money. ₹1,000 and ₹10,000 only was the January 1946 episode.

s: The demonetisation announced on 8 November 2016 primarily withdrew which notes from circulation?
x: The 2016 announcement withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, effective from midnight. New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were subsequently issued.

s: What was the legal basis cited for the 2016 demonetisation?
o: Section 26(2) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 10 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
x: The legal basis was Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, on the recommendation of the RBI’s Central Board.

s: Which authority issues the ₹1 note in India?
x: The ₹1 note and coins are issued by the Government of India; the remaining notes are issued by the RBI.

s: Under the Minimum Reserve System for note issue, of the ₹200 crore of gold and forex, what is the minimum value of gold that must be held?
x: The Minimum Reserve System needs ₹200 crore of gold and forex, of which ₹115 crore must be gold.

s: The 1978 demonetisation of high-denomination notes was carried out under which Prime Minister?
x: The High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978 came under Morarji Desai.

s: Which of the following pairs (year – notes demonetised) is correctly matched?
x: 1978 withdrew ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes; 2016 withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000, and 1946 withdrew ₹1,000 and ₹10,000.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 2016 demonetisation:
1. Curbing counterfeit currency (FICN) was one of its stated objectives.
2. The Supreme Court upheld it by a 4:1 majority in 2023.
3. The ₹2,000 notes withdrawn in May 2023 ceased to be legal tender.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Black money, FICN, corruption and terror financing were its objectives and the SC upheld it 4:1; the ₹2,000 notes withdrawn in May 2023 are still legal tender.

s: Which Act ended the liability on the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes after the 2016 demonetisation?
o: Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017
Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act
x: The Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 followed the 2016 demonetisation; the High Denomination Act was for 1978.

s: About what share of the currency in circulation, by value, was withdrawn by the 2016 demonetisation?
x: The ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes withdrawn in 2016 made up about 86% of currency by value.

s: According to the RBI, about what share of the notes demonetised in 2016 came back to banks?
x: About 99% of the demonetised notes returned to banks, as per the RBI.

s: According to NCRB's Crime in India 2024, fake Indian currency (FICN) worth about how much was seized?
x: NCRB recorded ₹54.61 crore of fake currency seized, mostly ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes.

s: Under which Act were the ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes demonetised in 1978?
o: Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act
x: The 1978 demonetisation under Morarji Desai was done through the High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act.

s: How were the high-denomination notes demonetised in January 1946?
x: The January 1946 demonetisation of ₹1,000 and ₹10,000 notes was done by an ordinance.

s: In December 2016, which country ordered its largest banknote, the 100-bolivar note, out of circulation?
x: Venezuela's President Maduro ordered the 100-bolivar note withdrawn in December 2016; the deadline was later put off after protests.

s: Which of the following monetary aggregates is the most liquid?
x: Liquidity declines in the order M1, M2, M3, M4, so M1 is the most liquid and M4 the least.

s: In Indian monetary statistics, by what name is M3 also known?
x: M3 is broad money and is described as aggregate monetary resources. It comprises M1 and time deposits with the banking system.

s: On whose recommendation was the present framework of monetary aggregates M1 to M4 introduced?
o: Second Working Group on Money Supply
x: The monetary aggregate framework from M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the Second Working Group on Money Supply in 1977.

s: Which is the most commonly used measure of broad money supply in India?
x: M3 (broad money) is the most used measure; M1 is narrow money and M0 is reserve money.

s: Which of the following components of money supply is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Demand deposits with banks – locked for a fixed period; least liquid
Time deposits with banks – locked for a fixed period; least liquid
Currency with the public – immediate cash in hand
Other deposits with RBI – balances of foreign central banks and international bodies
x: Demand deposits can be withdrawn instantly; it is time deposits that are locked for a fixed period and least liquid.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the new monetary aggregates from the liquidity aggregates proposed by the RBI working group?
o: NM0–NM3 are residency-based, while L1–L3 add specified broader liquidity components.
NM0–NM3 measure fiscal deficits, while L1–L3 measure public expenditure.
NM0–NM3 are confined to equity shares, while L1–L3 cover government securities.
NM0–NM3 consist only of foreign-exchange reserves, while L1–L3 consist only of coins.
x: NM0–NM3 are residency-based aggregates that distinguish short-term from long-term deposits. L1–L3 broaden the coverage by adding specified post-office, financial-institution and NBFC liabilities.

s: What does M3 minus M1 equal?
x: Since M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks, M3 − M1 equals time deposits.

s: What is added to M1 to get M2?
o: all post office deposits except NSCs
x: M2 = M1 + post office savings bank deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks.

s: Who chaired the RBI Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (1998)?
x: The 1998 (third) working group was chaired by Y. V. Reddy and proposed the residency-based NM0–NM3 and L1–L3.

s: Post-office deposits, term money and CDs of financial institutions, and public deposits of NBFCs are added in which aggregates?
x: The broader liquidity aggregates L1–L3 add post-office deposits, term money and CDs of FIs, and NBFC public deposits.

s: Which of the following describes the new monetary aggregates NM0–NM3 (1998)?
o: residency-based, separating short-term from long-term deposits
based on gold backing of currency
limited to currency with the public
x: NM0–NM3 are residency-based and separate short-term from long-term deposits.

s: M4 is M3 plus all post-office deposits, excluding which of the following?
x: M4 = M3 + all post-office deposits excluding NSCs.

s: Which of the following monetary aggregates are classed as narrow money?
x: M1 and M2 are narrow money; M3 and M4 are broad money.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. M2 is a measure of broad money.
2. M4 is the least liquid monetary aggregate.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: M2 is narrow money; M4 is broad and the least liquid (M1 > M2 > M3 > M4).

s: Which of the following about money supply measures is NOT correct?
o: M1 includes currency with the public
Time deposits with banks are part of M1
Other deposits with the RBI are part of both M1 and M3
M3 includes time deposits with banks
x: Time deposits are not part of M1 (currency, demand deposits and other RBI deposits); they are included in M3.

s: An increase in the SLR reduces the investible loan funds of commercial banks because it:
o: locks a greater percentage of bank funds in liquid assets
raises the rate at which banks borrow overnight
cuts the interest banks pay on deposits
lowers the currency held by the public
x: A higher SLR locks more of the banks' funds in liquid assets, leaving less to lend.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Increase in SLR – Reduces investible loan funds
CRR – Liquid assets held by the bank itself
SLR – Reserve maintained with the RBI
Decrease in SLR – Reduces investible loan funds
x: Raising SLR locks more funds in liquid assets and cuts loanable funds. SLR is held by the bank itself, CRR with the RBI, and an SLR cut frees funds.

s: Which of the following is a likely consequence of a high preference for cash in the economy?
o: An unlimited rise in the credit multiplier
A conversion of M3 into M0
A limitation on India’s credit multiplier
x: Weak banking habits and a high preference for cash raise the currency-deposit ratio, limiting the credit multiplier and the expansion of deposits.

s: With a reserve requirement of 10 per cent and no leakages, about how much in deposits can ₹100 of reserve money support?
x: With a 10 per cent reserve requirement, the simple deposit multiplier is 1/0.10, or 10. Thus, ₹100 of base money can support deposits approaching ₹1,000.

s: Who mainly creates deposit money by lending beyond required reserves?
x: The RBI creates reserve money by issuing notes, while commercial banks create deposit money by lending beyond their required CRR and SLR reserves.

s: If cdr is the currency-deposit ratio and rdr the reserve-deposit ratio, which formula gives the money multiplier (m)?
x: The money multiplier is m = (1 + cdr)/(cdr + rdr), so a higher cdr or rdr (CRR, SLR) lowers it. The second option is its reciprocal, and the other two are not the standard formula.

s: Which one of the following policy actions directly injects reserve money into the banking system?
o: RBI sells government securities in the open market
The public withdraws deposits as cash
RBI purchases government securities in the open market
x: An RBI purchase of government securities credits reserves to the banking system and injects reserve money, supporting an expansion of money supply.

s: How is the money multiplier represented?
x: The money multiplier is the ratio of total money supply to base money, i.e. M3 divided by M0.

s: When ₹1 lakh is withdrawn in cash from a demand deposit account, currency with the public rises by ₹1 lakh. What happens to demand deposits?
x: Demand deposits fall by ₹1 lakh as currency with the public rises by ₹1 lakh, so total money supply stays the same.

s: When the public deposits currency in banks, money supply:
x: Depositing currency only moves money from currency to deposits, so money supply does not rise.

s:
Consider the following statements about an increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio:
1. Banks have less money to lend.
2. The money multiplier rises.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: A higher CRR parks more bank money with the RBI, so banks have less to lend and the money multiplier falls.

s: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, placed India on which monetary standard?
x: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, put India on the gold standard.

s: In which year was the General Bank of Bengal and Bihar established?
x: It was set up in 1773, before the Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act (1899), transfer of note issue to the RBI (1935) and decimal coinage (1957).

s: The monopoly of note issue was given to the Government by which enactment?
o: Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899
x: The Paper Currency Act, 1861, gave the Government the monopoly of note issue, replacing the earlier private and presidency-bank pattern of issuance.

s: In which year was note issue transferred to the Reserve Bank of India?
x: Note issue passed to the RBI in 1935; 1861 gave the Government the monopoly of note issue.

s: Under which Act was decimal coinage introduced in India from 1 April 1957?
o: Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899
x: Decimal coinage came on 1 April 1957 under the Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955, with ₹1 = 100 naye paise.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Modern quantity theory – J. M. Keynes
Liquidity preference theory – J. M. Keynes
x: The modern quantity theory is associated with Milton Friedman, not Keynes; Keynes is linked with liquidity preference.

s: In the Cambridge cash-balance equation M = kPY, what does 'k' stand for?
o: The reciprocal of the velocity of money
x: In M = kPY, k equals 1/V, the reciprocal of velocity; Fisher's version is MV = PT.

s: With whom are monetarism and the role of money supply associated?
x: Milton Friedman is associated with monetarism; Hayek with liberal, market-based economics.

s: With whom is the IS-LM model associated?
x: Hicks gave the IS-LM model; Hawtrey gave the pure monetary trade-cycle theory and Hayek the Austrian cycle theory.

s: According to Keynes, the demand for money arises from the transactions, precautionary and which other motive?
x: Keynes's liquidity-preference theory names three motives: transactions, precautionary and speculative.

s: With whom is the quantity theory equation MV = PT associated?
x: MV = PT is Fisher's quantity theory; M = kPY is the Cambridge cash-balance equation of Marshall and Pigou.

s: With whom is the inventory (square-root rule) model of transactions demand for money associated?
x: The inventory model was given by Baumol (1952) and Tobin (1956).

s: How does the speculative demand for money vary with the rate of interest?
x: Speculative demand varies inversely with interest; at higher interest rates money demand falls.

s: If the supply of money remains fixed and the demand for money falls, what happens to the rate of interest?
o: It first rises and then falls
x: With fixed money supply, a rise in money demand raises the interest rate and a fall in demand lowers it.

s: With which school of trade cycle theory is Friedrich Hayek associated?
x: Hayek gave the Austrian cycle theory and backed free-market economics.

s: Who gave the principle of effective demand?
x: The principle of effective demand is Keynes's.

s: What does currency in circulation include?
o: Notes, foreign exchange assets and bankers' deposits
Notes, demand deposits and time deposits
Rupee coins, government securities and small coins
Notes, rupee coins and small coins
x: Currency in circulation comprises notes, rupee coins and small coins. It is held partly by the public and partly as cash in hand with banks.

s: By what other name is high-powered money known?
x: High-powered money is also called reserve money, monetary base and central bank money; bank money is secondary money.

s: On the uses side, high-powered money comprises currency held by the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with the RBI and which of the following?
x: The uses-side composition of high-powered money is currency with the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with RBI and other deposits with RBI.

s: Which of the following is a component on the sources side of reserve money?
o: Net foreign exchange assets of the RBI
x: Net forex assets of the RBI are on the sources side; the other three are on the uses side.

s: 'Other deposits with the RBI', a part of high-powered money, include the deposits of which of the following?
x: Other deposits include those of quasi-government bodies, FIs, foreign central banks and governments, and international agencies such as the IMF; banks' deposits are bankers' deposits.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes M0 or reserve money?
o: M3 + all post office deposits excluding NSCs
Currency in circulation + bankers’ deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
M1 + post office savings bank deposits
Currency with the public + demand deposits + time deposits
x: M0, or reserve money, consists of currency in circulation, bankers’ deposits with the RBI and other deposits with the RBI. It is the monetary base.

s: The Cash Reserve Ratio was reduced by 100 basis points to what level of Net Demand and Time Liabilities, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore?
x: The CRR was reduced by 100 basis points to 3.0 per cent of NDTL, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore by December 2025.

s: When did the retail pilot of the e-Rupee (CBDC) begin?
x: The wholesale pilot began in November 2022 and the retail pilot in December 2022.

s: Which of the following is NOT an identified feature or use of the e-Rupee?
o: Mandatory replacement of all bank deposits
Programmable money for direct benefit transfer
A cross-border pilot with the UAE
x: Offline payments, programmability for DBT and a UAE cross-border pilot are identified uses; mandatory replacement of bank deposits is not.

s: When did the wholesale pilot of the e-Rupee (CBDC) begin?
x: The wholesale pilot began in November 2022 and the retail pilot in December 2022.

s: What was the money multiplier in India as on 31 December 2025?
x: On 31 Dec 2025 the money multiplier stood at 6.21.

s: The e-Rupee (CBDC) is a direct liability of which institution?
x: The e-Rupee is legal tender and a direct liability of the RBI, whereas UPI money is a liability of banks.

s: In 2026, where was the Digital Food Currency pilot using the e-Rupee launched?
x: The Digital Food Currency pilot based on the e-Rupee was launched in Puducherry in 2026.

s: In May 2026, about how many banknotes were in circulation in India?
x: In May 2026, about 174 billion notes worth over ₹42.12 lakh crore were in circulation.

s: Banks may maintain their SLR in cash, gold, other approved securities and which of the following?
o: Unencumbered Government securities and Treasury Bills
x: SLR is held by banks themselves in cash, gold, unencumbered government securities (including T-Bills and SDLs) and approved securities.

s: Which ratio is maintained by banks as a cash balance with the RBI and earns no interest?
x: CRR is kept as a cash balance with the RBI and earns no interest; SLR is held by the bank itself in cash, gold and eligible securities.

s: What is the statutory range of the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)?
x: SLR can be set between 0% and 40% of NDTL; the earlier 25% floor was removed by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007.

s: On whose advice was the SLR gradually reduced from its 1991-92 level?
x: The SLR was gradually reduced after the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee on financial-sector reforms.

s: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is governed by which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
x: CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act; SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

s: The SLR, which was 38.5 per cent in 1991–92, stood at what level in September 2023?
x: The SLR was 18 per cent in September 2023, down from 38.5 per cent in 1991–92.

s: In the context of RBI's monetary policy instruments, the term 'required reserve ratio' refers to which one of the following?
x: The required reserve ratio is the CRR: the share of NDTL banks must keep as a cash balance with the RBI (Sec 42, RBI Act), earning no interest. SLR is a liquidity ratio held by banks themselves in cash, gold and approved securities, not a reserve with the RBI. CRAR and LCR are Basel prudential ratios on capital and liquidity, not reserve requirements.

s: Which reserve requirement controls liquidity, acts as a liquidity buffer and is held in assets that can earn returns?
x: SLR assets such as government bonds earn returns, and SLR controls liquidity and acts as a buffer; CRR controls liquidity and credit.

s: Which Act removed the 25 per cent statutory floor on SLR?
x: The BR (Amendment) Act, 2007 removed the 25% SLR floor; SLR now ranges 0–40% of NDTL.

s: What is the initial penalty on a bank for an SLR shortfall?
x: An SLR shortfall attracts bank rate + 3%, rising to bank rate + 5% if it continues.

s:
Consider the following statements about the SLR:
1. MSS securities count towards the SLR.
2. The SLR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: MSS securities count towards SLR; SLR is under Section 24 of the BR Act 1949, while Section 42 of the RBI Act governs CRR.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934.
2. The CRR has a statutory floor of 3% and a ceiling of 20%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: CRR comes under Section 42 of the RBI Act; since 2006 it has no floor or ceiling. It is SLR that has a 0-40% range.

s: At what rate was the temporary incremental CRR (I-CRR) announced by the RBI on 10 August 2023 set?
x: The temporary I-CRR was 10%, announced on 10 August 2023; it impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore.

s: About how much did the temporary 10 per cent incremental CRR of August 2023 impound?
x: The I-CRR of 10 Aug 2023 impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore.

s: In which year was the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) introduced?
x: MSF came in 2011, after LAF (2000) and MSS (2004), and before MCLR (2016).

s: In which year was the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) introduced?
x: LAF came in 2000; MSS in 2004, MSF in 2011 and SDF in 2022.

s: What is the upper end of the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor?
x: The MSF rate forms the upper end of the corridor; the repo rate is the overnight lending rate against approved collateral.

s:
Consider the following statements about the LAF corridor:
1. The SDF forms the floor of the corridor.
2. The repo rate lies above the MSF rate.
3. The MSF and the bank rate are aligned at the ceiling.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The SDF is the floor, the repo rate lies above it, and the MSF and bank rate sit at the ceiling; statement 2 is wrong because the repo rate is below the MSF.

s: How is the fixed-rate reverse repo different from the SDF?
o: Permits banks to borrow by dipping into SLR
Absorbs funds against Government securities and is used at RBI's discretion
Requires banks to maintain cash with RBI without interest
Lends funds to banks without collateral
x: The fixed-rate reverse repo absorbs funds against Government securities and is now used at the RBI's discretion, while the SDF absorbs funds without collateral.

s: Under the current MSF arrangement, up to what share of NDTL may banks dip into their SLR holdings?
x: The MSF rate is repo plus 25 bps with an SLR dip of up to 2% of NDTL; the older design had a 100-bps spread and a 1% limit.

s: If the repo rate is 5.25 per cent, what would be the MSF rate under the current corridor?
x: The MSF rate is 25 basis points above repo (5.50%), and the SDF rate 25 basis points below it (5.00%).

s: Which of the following about the Reverse Repo is NOT correct?
o: Under it, banks borrow from the RBI
It is used to absorb surplus liquidity
It is a monetary policy tool
Under it, the RBI borrows from banks
x: Under reverse repo the RBI borrows from banks to absorb surplus liquidity; banks borrowing from the RBI is repo.

s: What is the RBI's principal policy lending rate?
x: Repo is the main policy lending rate and the tool for regular liquidity; MSF is for emergency, marginal needs.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Repo – principal policy rate for regular liquidity management
Marginal Standing Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity from banks without collateral
Bank Rate – rate at which the RBI rediscounts bills of exchange
Standing Deposit Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral
x: MSF is overnight emergency borrowing above the repo rate that lets banks dip into SLR; absorbing surplus liquidity without collateral is the SDF.

s: Which of the following about the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is NOT correct?
o: It is an overnight borrowing facility
Banks borrow from the RBI under it
Its rate is usually repo plus 0.25%
Its rate is lower than the repo rate
x: MSF costs more than repo, usually repo plus 0.25%; it is an overnight emergency window, while repo is for regular liquidity.

s: Which of the following monetary-policy stances is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Neutral – rates can move either way, depending on the data
Accommodative – supports growth with ample liquidity; rate cuts likely
Calibrated tightening – no cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
Hawkish – worried about growth, with a bias towards easing
x: A hawkish stance worries about inflation and tightens; concern for growth with an easing bias is dovish.

s: Which of the following is used by the RBI to absorb surplus liquidity?
x: Absorbing surplus liquidity is the role of reverse repo; the Bank Rate is the RBI's long-term rediscount rate on bills of exchange and commercial paper.

s: When the MSF began in May 2011, by how much above the repo rate was its rate set?
x: MSF began in May 2011 at repo + 100 bps; it is now repo + 25 bps.

s: When was the MSF rate aligned with the Bank Rate?
x: The MSF was aligned to the Bank Rate in February 2012.

s: Among NBFCs, which entities can access the RBI's LAF?
x: Only Primary Dealers, classed as NBFCs, have access to the LAF.

s: A 'hawkish' monetary-policy stance indicates that the central bank:
